sak1: Is a stabbing pain low in your back, on one side, coming from the sacroiliac joint? Symptoms, causes, why diagnosis is difficult, treatment options and six exercises to do at home.
sak3: Do you have a stabbing pain at the very bottom of your back, on one side, at the upper back of your hip? Does it get worse when you get up from a chair or after sitting for a long time? This pain may be coming from the sacroiliac joint, which connects the lower end of the spine to the pelvis. This joint is estimated to play a part in about 15 to 30 per cent of cases of low back pain. It is hard to diagnose, but most people get relief with exercise and physiotherapy.

sak35: How can you tell the pain is coming from this joint?
sak36: It is not easy. The pain is very similar to pain from the lower back, the hip or the sciatic nerve. No single examination test or scan gives a definite answer; doctors look at several pain provocation tests together. The most reliable method is usually to inject a local anaesthetic into the joint and see whether the pain goes away.
sak38: Sacroiliac belts are among the options used alongside exercise, physiotherapy and injections, but results vary from person to person. You can assess whether a belt works for you together with a physiotherapist.
sak39: For very few people. A fusion operation is considered for pain that has not settled despite at least 6 months of non-surgical treatment and has been shown by tests and a diagnostic injection to come from the joint. For some people, radiofrequency treatment, which uses heat to switch off the nerve endings, can bring relief lasting 6–12 months.
